input.question: Why are there so many new medical breakthroughs in the news, but practically none of them ever become legitimate cures.
input.ground_truth: Because a breakthrough towards a cure is just one brick in the road, but it's what gets highly touted by the media because it's easy to point out. A team of scientists working in lab conditions come up with something promising and release their findings. Someone in the media sees this paper and turns "Disease has possible vulnerability!" and turns it into "CURE IS IMMINENT!!!1!" What they don't say is that it will take another few years of research, plus another few years of study, then another few years to create a human-safe cure (doesn't do anyone any good to cure the disease if it kills the patient as well), and then a few more years to figure out how to produce it at profitable levels.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Why are there so many new medical breakthroughs in the news, but practically none of them ever become legitimate cures.

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you are playing with your building blocks. Sometimes, you try a new way to stack them and it looks really cool, but it falls down. That’s like a new idea in medicine. Scientists try new things all the time, like building with blocks, to see if they can help people feel better.

But just because something looks cool or works a little bit in the beginning doesn’t mean it will always work every time. Most of the time, the new idea doesn’t turn into a real, perfect solution. It might help a little, or it might not work at all. Scientists have to try the new idea lots and lots of times, with lots of people, to make sure it really works and is safe.

So, lots of new ideas (medical breakthroughs) are shared in the news, but only the ones that really work after lots of checking become real cures that help everyone. It’s like finding the best way to build a super strong tower with your blocks!
